claim: Grid cells are found in the medial entorhinal cortex (MEC) and para-subiculum.
source: 308 grid cells recorded over multiple days in the medial entorhinal cortex (MEC) and/or para-subiculum (Figure 1F) of the seven rats
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the anatomical locations where grid cells were recorded, supported by histological data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Grid cells fire in space according to a periodic, triangular pattern.
source: a grid cell fires in space according to a periodic, triangular pattern that simultaneously reveals its positional (by its phase) and directional (by its orientation) anchoring to the external world
evidence: This is a direct statement in the manuscript describing the fundamental firing property of grid cells.

claim: Grid cells do not undergo global remapping but are active with similar spatial correlates in all environments.
source: Unlike place cells, grid cells do not undergo 'global remapping' (Leutgeb et al., 2004), but instead they are active and have similar spatial correlates in all environments (Hafting et al., 2005; Fyhn et al., 2007; Marozzi et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies that established this property of grid cells.

claim: Following a 20° clockwise platform rotation (ROT20), grid cells systematically under-rotated with respect to the platform rotation angle.
source: a reliable influence of the room was still detectable, as the grids systematically under-rotated with respect to the platform rotation angle (20°) (mean rotation = 14° CW, 109 units pooled from five rats, p<0.0001
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative measurements from 109 grid cells showing statistically significant under-rotation.

claim: The phase shift of grid cells in ROT20 was very small (mean ± S.D., 3.5 ± 4.0 cm, 5 ± 5% of grid period).
source: In contrast to the grid rotations, the shift of grid phases in ROT20 was very small (mean ± S.D., 3.5 ± 4.0 cm, 5 ± 5% of grid period, Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement reported in the text and illustrated in Figure 2C.

claim: Grid rotations in response to the ROT70 manipulation formed a bimodal distribution.
source: In contrast to the uniform response to the ROT20 manipulation, grid rotations in response to the ROT70 manipulation formed a bimodal distribution (Figure 3A).
evidence: This observation is directly stated and shown in Figure 3A displaying two distinct modes of grid rotation responses.

claim: One mode of the ROT70 response (left mode, 50 units from three rats) was located at ~20° CCW, representing grids controlled by the platform's geometric structure.
source: One of the modes ('left mode', 50 units from three rats) was located at ~20° CCW (mean 18°), representing grids that were controlled by the platform's geometric structure (the 'geometric' reference frame), but rotated relative to the physical platform itself (test of mean angle vs. 10° CW, p<0.0001
evidence: This describes one mode of the bimodal distribution with specific quantitative measurements and statistical testing.

claim: The other mode in ROT70 (right mode, mean 6° CW, 69 units from three rats) reflects grids that kept a stronger relationship with the room's distal landmarks/walls than with the platform's geometric boundaries.
source: the other mode in Figure 3A ('right mode', mean 6° CW, 69 units from three rats) reflects grids that kept a stronger relationship with the room's distal landmarks/walls than with the platform's geometric boundaries (Figure 3D).
evidence: This describes the second mode of the bimodal distribution with quantitative data and visual examples in Figure 3D.

claim: For grids in the right mode of ROT70, phase shifts were much larger when calculated relative to the physical platform compared to the room (29 ± 12.9 cm vs. 6 ± 3.7 cm, p<7.5x10−13).
source: The phase shifts necessary to align each STD grid to its corresponding ROT70 grid were much larger when calculated relative to the physical platform compared to the room, both in absolute space and as a proportion of the grid period (phase shift magnitude, 29 ± 12.9 cm vs. 6 ± 3.7 cm, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, W(69) = 8, p<7.5x10−13
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison with statistical testing demonstrating room-based control of these grids.

claim: In the translation manipulation (SHIFT), the firing patterns expressed by grid cells on the platform displayed a striking degree of similarity between STD and SHIFT.
source: In the translation manipulation (SHIFT, 119 units from seven rats), the platform was shifted by half its length along the room's longer axis (Figure 1C). The firing patterns expressed by grid and other spatial cells on the platform displayed a striking degree of similarity between STD and SHIFT (Figure 4A–C)
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and illustrated with examples in Figures 4A-C.

claim: In SHIFT, room-relative phase shifts were much larger than platform-based phase shifts (14 ± 10.1 vs. 5 ± 2.6 cm, p<4.6x10−16).
source: The room-relative phase shifts were much larger than the platform-based phase shifts, both in absolute space and as a proportion of the grid period (phase shift magnitude, 14 ± 10.1 vs. 5 ± 2.6 cm, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, W(119) = 507, p<4.6x10−16
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison with statistical testing showing platform-based control in the SHIFT condition.

claim: Room-bound correlations were dramatically lower than platform-bound correlations in SHIFT (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, W(119) = 68, p<1.5x10−20).
source: The room-bound correlations were dramatically lower than the platform-bound correlations (Figure 4E, red vs. blue; Wilcoxon signed-rank test, W(119) = 68, p<1.5x10−20).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of correlations shown in Figure 4E demonstrating platform control.

claim: Relative to the platform frame of reference, grids generally shifted slightly in the direction opposite to the performed translation in SHIFT.
source: Relative to the platform frame of reference, grids generally shifted slightly in the direction opposite to the performed translation, thus 'lagging' behind the platform (Figure 4F, examples in Figure 4A). The component of the grid phase shift relative to the platform along this axis was significant (t-test against 0, t118 = 10.85, p<1.8x10−19
evidence: This describes a systematic under-translation with statistical testing and visual examples.

claim: Grids tended to perform a small rotation in the CCW direction in SHIFT (mean 2° CCW).
source: Moreover, grids tended to perform a small rotation in the CCW direction (mean 2° CCW; Figure 4G; examples in Figure 4B). This small CCW re-orientation was significant at p<0.01 in 4 of the five rats with n > 7
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement with statistical testing across multiple rats.

claim: Grid rotation responses to each manipulation type were highly consistent over one week or longer (mean vector length >0.92 in all 10 rat-manipulation couplings).
source: The mean vector length in each coupling was very high (>0.92), demonstrating that the responses to each manipulation type were highly consistent over one week or longer.
evidence: This quantifies the reproducibility of grid responses across multiple recording days.

claim: In rat 387, the equilateral-triangular grid pattern was often selectively disrupted in ROT70.
source: In one rat (rat 387, platform with lips), the equilateral-triangular grid pattern was often selectively disrupted in ROT70, even though the cell continued to fire in discrete, multiple fields (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes a specific observation in one rat with visual examples provided.

claim: In rat 387, 44% of ROT70 sessions passed the gridness test compared to 64% in all other sessions (χ2(1)=5.3, p<0.021).
source: Whereas 19/43 (44%) of the ROT70 sessions passed the gridness test, a larger proportion did so in all other sessions (84/131, 64%, χ2 test for proportions with Yates correction for continuity: χ2(1)=5.3, p<0.021).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of gridness test pass rates between conditions.

claim: In rat 292, STD sessions repeated at the end of the day (STD2) consistently displayed a different alignment of the grid compared to the first STD sessions of the same day.
source: In another rat (rat 292, platform with walls), STD sessions repeated at the end of the day (STD2) consistently displayed a different alignment of the grid compared to the first STD sessions of the same day (Figure 6B (i)).
evidence: This describes a specific phenomenon observed in one rat with visual examples.

claim: In rat 292, STD2 invariably reproduced the grid-platform alignment that was displayed in a previous, noncontiguous rotation manipulation.
source: This realignment was not random; rather, STD2 invariably reproduced the grid-platform alignment that was displayed in a previous, noncontiguous rotation manipulation (Figure 6B (i)).
evidence: This describes the specific pattern of realignment observed in STD2 sessions.

claim: In rat 292, some boundary cells did not change their firing patterns between STD and STD2 when simultaneously recorded grid cells realigned.
source: Third, some boundary cells did not change their firing patterns between STD and STD2 when the simultaneously recorded grid cells realigned. Instead, these cells continued to fire along the same geometric boundary in both sessions (Figure 6B (ii)), thus dissociating from the grids in these and other sessions
evidence: This describes a dissociation between grid cells and boundary cells observed in simultaneous recordings.

claim: Examples of divergence between grid and boundary representations were observed in rat 377 when the grid strongly dissociated from the platform reference frame.
source: Examples of divergence between grid and boundary representations were also observed in a second rat (rat 377, platform with lips) when the grid strongly dissociated from the platform reference frame (the 'right mode' of Figure 3A,D). In this situation some boundary cells kept firing along the same geometric boundary (i.e., the boundary representation tracked the proximal geometric reference frame, unlike the grid representation) (Figure 7B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes grid-boundary dissociation observed in a second rat with visual examples.

claim: Correlations between rate maps from the first and second halves of sessions were high in both STD (median >0.68) and manipulated sessions (median >0.69) across four rats.
source: These correlations were found to be high in both STD (median correlation >0.68 in each rat) and manipulated sessions (median correlation >0.69 in each rat), suggesting that there was no major intra-session grid drift or change of anchoring within a session (correlations in STD were not different from those in manipulated sessions: Mann-Whitney test, U = 32572, p>0.48, all rats pooled together).
evidence: This quantifies the stability of grid patterns within individual recording sessions.

claim: Of 476 grid cell pairs from six rats, 81% displayed a rotation difference <5° and 88% had joint correlation >0.7.
source: Of the 476 pairs from six rats, 81% displayed a rotation difference <5° and 88% had joint correlation >0.7 (Figure 8A), indicating high levels of geometric coordination.
evidence: This quantifies the geometric coordination between simultaneously recorded grid cells.

claim: Grid pairs segregated into three clusters according to their grid scale ratio (SR1-3: 336, 135, and five pairs, respectively).
source: Because of the discrete representation of spatial scale in the grid system (Barry et al., 2007; Stensola et al., 2012), grid pairs segregated into three clusters according to their grid scale ratio (Figure 8A, SR1-3: 336, 135, and five pairs, respectively).
evidence: This describes the clustering of grid pairs by scale ratio with specific counts.

claim: The distributions of rotation difference and joint correlation for SR1 vs SR2 diverged minimally (difference of medians for rotation difference = 1.1°, p<0.0005; difference of medians for joint correlation = 0.02, p<0.0008).
source: The distributions of rotation difference and joint correlation for SR1 vs SR2 diverged minimally (Figure 8B, blue vs. red solid curves; difference of medians for the rotation difference measure = 1.1°, Mann-Whitney test, U = 18012, p<0.0005 [lost significance in thinned datasets n1 = 62, n2 = 42, p>0.5]; difference of medians for the joint correlation = 0.02, U = 27202, p<0.0008)
evidence: This quantifies the similarity of coordination between same-scale and different-scale grid pairs.

claim: Place cells represent the animal's position allocentrically, similar to a 'you are here' mark on a geographic map.
source: These cells signal the animal's position or direction relative to the external world; that is, they represent space allocentrically, similar to a 'you are here' mark on a geographic map.
evidence: This is a conceptual description of how spatial cells encode position, drawing on established knowledge.

claim: The allocentric property of spatial cells has implicated them as the neural substrate of a 'cognitive map' of the environment.
source: The allocentric property has implicated these cells as the neural substrate of a 'cognitive map' of the environment (O'Keefe and Nadel, 1978; but see Bennett, 1996; Filimon, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to foundational work on the cognitive map theory.

claim: Behavioral and electrophysiological studies have inferred two major allocentric determinants of the internal map's reference frame: distal landmarks and the geometric configuration of proximal boundaries.
source: Behavioral studies (Cheng, 1986; Hamilton et al., 2007; Tommasi et al., 2012) and electrophysiological studies of place cells (O'Keefe and Conway, 1978; Knierim and Rao, 2003; Siegel et al., 2008; Samsonovich and McNaughton, 1997; O'Keefe and Burgess, 1996) and head direction (HD) cells (Taube et al., 1990b; Zugaro et al., 2001) inferred two major allocentric determinants of the internal map's reference frame: distal (inaccessible) landmarks and the geometric configuration of the proximal (accessible) boundaries defining the animal's navigation range.
evidence: This claim synthesizes findings from multiple cited studies across different cell types.

claim: Grid cells are presumed to provide a universal metric for the animal's movements in space and for the cognitive map.
source: Grid cells are presumed to provide a universal metric for the animal's movements in space and for the cognitive map (Moser et al., 2008; but see Krupic et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to theoretical work, with a contrasting view also cited.

claim: Studies to date have mostly concentrated on the role of proximal navigation boundaries in the anchoring, shaping, compartmentalization, and metrical correction of the grid pattern.
source: Studies to date have mostly concentrated on the role of the proximal navigation boundaries and their geometric configuration in the anchoring (Savelli et al., 2008; Solstad et al., 2008; Stensola et al., 2012, 2015; Krupic et al., 2015), shaping (Barry et al., 2007; Stensola et al., 2015; Krupic et al., 2015), compartmentalization (Derdikman et al., 2009; Carpenter et al., 2015), and metrical correction (Hardcastle et al., 2015) of the grid pattern.
evidence: This summarizes the focus of previous grid cell research with multiple supporting citations.

claim: The influence of remote cues on grid cells remains under-investigated.
source: In contrast, the influence of remote cues remains under-investigated. Although grids were shown to realign or rescale in a context- or novelty-dependent manner after all distal cues were changed (Fyhn et al., 2007; Barry et al., 2007), the cues were not subject to spatial manipulations in these experiments (but see Neunuebel et al., 2013; Gupta et al., 2014 for experiments with circular tracks and T-mazes).
evidence: This identifies a gap in the literature that the current study addresses, with citations to relevant prior work.

claim: The experimental room was 355 × 280 cm with visually prominent cues affixed to the walls.
source: Visually prominent cues were affixed to the walls of the experimental room (355 × 280 cm, Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This describes the physical dimensions and features of the experimental apparatus.

claim: Two types of platforms were used: one with walls (35.6 cm) and replaceable floor paper (five rats), and one with small lips (2.5 cm) and non-replaceable floor (two rats).
source: Two types of platforms were used with two separate sets of rats. One had walls (35.6 cm) and replaceable floor paper producing a luminance contrast between the walls and the floor (five rats, Figure 1D, left). The other had small lips (2.5 cm) around the perimeter and its floor was not replaceable (two rats, Figure 1D, right).
evidence: This describes the two apparatus types used in the experiments.

claim: The square foraging platform was 137 × 137 cm.
source: We translated or rotated a square foraging platform (137 × 137 cm) between recording sessions
evidence: This specifies the dimensions of the platform used in experiments.

claim: 308 grid cells were recorded from seven rats.
source: Results from all 308 grid cells recorded over multiple days in the medial entorhinal cortex (MEC) and/or para-subiculum (Figure 1F) of the seven rats are described
evidence: This states the total number of grid cells and rats in the study.

claim: The difference in dominant reference frame between the two modes of ROT70 is unlikely to result from sampling of functionally differentiated neuronal networks.
source: The difference of response expressed by the bimodal distribution of rotations in ROT70 (Figure 3A) is unlikely to result from the sampling of functionally differentiated neuronal networks (Table 1).
evidence: This inference is supported by anatomical distribution data shown in Table 1.

claim: The same brain areas are represented in both modes of the ROT70 response, sometimes in multiple rats and by multiple tetrodes in the same rat.
source: Note that the same brain areas are represented in both modes, sometimes in multiple rats and by multiple tetrodes in the same rat. The different response accounted by the two modes is therefore unlikely to depend on a functional differentiation across brain areas or within the same area.
evidence: This is stated in the caption of Table 1 and supported by the anatomical distribution data.

claim: Grid coordination was very high regardless of the extent of the animal's previous experience with the manipulation.
source: Furthermore, grid coordination was very high regardless of the extent of the animal's previous experience with the manipulation (Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This finding is stated and supported by data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: Grid cells of similar spacing remain rigidly coupled during manipulations that elicit their global realignment or rescaling.
source: Grids of similar spacing remain rigidly coupled during manipulations that elicit their global realignment or rescaling, including during hippocampal remapping (Fyhn et al., 2007; Yoon et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Simultaneously recorded grid cells responded consistently to the conflicting cues, even when their responses implied a large collective drift from the familiar reference frames.
source: Simultaneously recorded grid cells responded consistently to the conflicting cues, even when their responses implied a large collective drift from the familiar reference frames.
evidence: This summarizes a key finding about grid cell coordination during cue conflict.

claim: Grid coordination was found to be very high even for grids of markedly distinct scale.
source: Grid coordination was found to be very high even for grids of markedly distinct scale (Barry et al., 2007; Stensola et al., 2012).
evidence: This finding is stated with citations to previous work on grid scale organization.

claim: The present experiments demonstrate that the world lying beyond current navigation boundaries contributes to determining the allocentric reference frame of two-dimensional grid maps.
source: The present experiments demonstrate that the world lying beyond current navigation boundaries contributes to determining the allocentric reference frame of two-dimensional grid maps.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated at the beginning of the Discussion section.

claim: While platform geometry usually exerted a dominant influence on the grids, in some cases the grid map appeared embedded in the metric structure of the room and dissociated from the platform.
source: While platform geometry usually exerted a dominant—but rarely absolute—influence on the grids, in some cases the grid map appeared embedded in the metric structure of the room and dissociated from the platform (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This summarizes a key finding with references to supporting figures.

claim: Neural correlates of boundaries could decouple from the grids, reflecting the ability of the grid map to dissociate geometrically from real-world boundaries.
source: Neural correlates of boundaries could also decouple from the grids, reflecting further the ability of the grid map to dissociate geometrically from real-world boundaries.
evidence: This summarizes the finding of grid-boundary dissociation observed in the experiments.

claim: Grid cell properties can be reconciled with those of place cells, which have long been known to respond to both extra- and intra-maze inputs.
source: Grid cell properties can be reconciled or contrasted with those of place cells, which have long been known to respond to both extra- and intra-maze inputs (e.g, Kelemen and Fenton, 2010; see Knierim and Hamilton, 2011 for extensive review).
evidence: This claim draws a parallel between grid cells and place cells, supported by citations.

claim: Early place cell studies emphasized the importance of distal cues, but later studies documented the importance of local cues.
source: Early place cell studies emphasized the importance of distal cues (O'Keefe and Conway, 1978), but later studies amply documented the importance of local cues (Shapiro et al., 1997; Knierim, 2002; Knierim and Rao, 2003; Lee et al., 2004; Renaudineau et al., 2007; Siegel et al., 2008; Kelemen and Fenton, 2010), including geometric ones (O'Keefe and Burgess, 1996).
evidence: This summarizes the historical progression of place cell research with multiple citations.

claim: The observations motivate a similar revision/expansion of early grid cell studies focusing almost exclusively on the influence of local, geometric cues.
source: Our observations motivate a similar revision/expansion, in reverse, of the early grid cell studies focusing almost exclusively on the influence of local, geometric cues (Barry et al., 2007; Savelli et al., 2008; Derdikman et al., 2009; Stensola et al., 2012; Carpenter et al., 2015; Stensola et al., 2015; Krupic et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference about the implications of the current findings for the field, supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Differences in the relative dominance of distal and local cues appeared to depend on individual differences between rats and/or the type of apparatus, rather than on the anatomical regions where the grid cells were recorded.
source: In our experiments differences in the relative dominance of distal and local cues appeared to depend on individual differences between rats and/or the type of apparatus, rather than on the anatomical regions where the grid cells were recorded (Table 1, Figure 8).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data, with references to supporting figures and tables.

claim: A grid cell system subject to distal control is ideally suited to fit Tolman's original inspiration for the cognitive map as a 'comprehensive-map'.
source: Moreover, a grid cell system subject to distal control is ideally suited to fit Tolman's original inspiration for the cognitive map as a 'comprehensive-map' (Tolman, 1948, p. 193).
evidence: This is a theoretical inference connecting the findings to Tolman's cognitive map theory.

claim: Rats' ability to take novel shortcuts through previously inaccessible regions led Tolman to hypothesize the 'building up in the nervous system' of allocentric maps.
source: Rats' ability to take novel shortcuts through previously inaccessible regions led Tolman to hypothesize the 'building up in the nervous system' of such allocentric maps (Tolman, 1948, p. 193).
evidence: This is a historical claim about Tolman's theory, supported by citation.

claim: Grid cell-based path planning is theoretically possible and robust to grid distortions such as shearing and boundary-induced perturbations.
source: Grid cell-based path planning is theoretically possible (e.g, Kubie and Fenton, 2012; Erdem and Hasselmo, 2012; Bush et al., 2015) and robust to grid distortions such as shearing and boundary-induced perturbations (Stemmler et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical and modeling studies.

claim: Planning a path between two familiar regions through territory that was previously blocked off could in principle be accomplished via grid cells controlled by a distal reference frame comprising both regions.
source: Planning a path between two familiar regions through territory that was previously blocked off, therefore, could in principle be accomplished via grid cells controlled by a distal reference frame comprising both regions.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about potential grid cell function based on the findings.

claim: Interindividual variability in shortcut errors is consistent with the observation that the grid cell map can be, but is not always, controlled by the distal laboratory reference frame.
source: In this sense, interindividual variability in the shortcut errors (Tolman, 1948, see also Grieves and Dudchenko, 2013) is consistent with our observation that the grid cell map can be, but is not always, controlled by the distal laboratory reference frame, possibly with an associated angular error.
evidence: This connects behavioral observations to the current findings through inference.

claim: A remotely anchored grid map provides an implicit metric of currently inaccessible regions of the environment, which can later facilitate the pursuit of unanticipated navigation goals and opportunities.
source: In this putative framework, a remotely anchored grid map provides an implicit metric of currently inaccessible regions of the environment, which can later facilitate the pursuit of unanticipated navigation goals and opportunities.
evidence: This is a speculative functional interpretation of the findings.

claim: This framework differs from the hypothesis that the grid cell system is primarily dedicated to encoding the geometry of local enclosures.
source: This framework differs from the hypothesis that the grid cell system is primarily dedicated to encoding the geometry of local enclosures (Krupic et al., 2015, 2016)
evidence: This contrasts the current interpretation with an alternative hypothesis from the literature.

claim: The response of grid cells to the conflicting reference frames was diverse in frame preference, extent of under/over rotation/translation, and, in one rat, grid regularity.
source: The response of grid cells to the conflicting reference frames was diverse in frame preference, extent of under/over rotation/translation, and, in one rat, grid regularity.
evidence: This summarizes the diversity of grid cell responses observed in the experiments.

claim: These differences were generally manipulation-specific and consistent over many recording days.
source: These differences were generally manipulation-specific and consistent over many recording days.
evidence: This describes the reproducibility of the diverse responses.

claim: The repeatable phenomena possibly reflect an underlying discriminating process of the type that is hypothesized to produce different place cell maps and context-dependent memories through global remapping.
source: Rather, these repeatable phenomena possibly reflect an underlying discriminating process of the type that is hypothesized to produce different place cell maps and context-dependent memories through global remapping of place cell's firing locations (Nadel et al., 1985; Anderson et al., 2006; Colgin et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2012; Fyhn et al., 2007; Stensola et al., 2015; Stensola and Moser, 2016).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation connecting the findings to theories of remapping and memory.

claim: Previous observations include findings that global remapping or contextual changes are accompanied by grid realignment or expansion relative to a local enclosure.
source: Previous observations inspiring this hypothesis include the findings that global remapping or contextual changes are accompanied by grid realignment or expansion relative to a local enclosure (Fyhn et al., 2007; Barry et al., 2012; Marozzi et al., 2015)
evidence: This cites previous findings that support the interpretation.

claim: Global remapping can be elicited through the partial inactivation of MEC.
source: and that global remapping can be elicited through the partial inactivation of MEC (Miao et al., 2015; Rueckemann et al., 2016).
evidence: This cites experimental evidence linking MEC to remapping.

claim: The rats may have come to recognize and memorize each manipulation type as a separate experience or spatial context.
source: In our experiments, the rats may have come to recognize and memorize each manipulation type as a separate experience or spatial context, which was consistently rendered by a reproducible change of dominant reference frame or (more often) by a distinct anchoring of the grid map to the same dominant reference frame.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of why responses were manipulation-specific.

claim: The highly selective grid disruption in one rat cannot be attributed to tensions induced by the platform frame alone but probably to the grid system's attempt to reconcile proximal and distal inputs.
source: Thus the grid disruption cannot be attributed to tensions induced by the platform frame alone (Barry et al., 2007; Derdikman et al., 2009; Stensola et al., 2012; Krupic et al., 2015) but probably to the grid system's attempt to reconcile proximal and distal inputs.
evidence: This is an inference about the cause of grid disruption, contrasting with previous explanations.

claim: It is perhaps surprising that this response appeared to be consolidated instead of being corrected over the course of weeks of experience.
source: It is perhaps surprising that this response (as well as other seemingly 'dysfunctional' adaptations that we observed, such as under-rotations/translations) appeared to be consolidated instead of being corrected over the course of weeks of experience, similar to previous observations of grid distortions (Derdikman et al., 2009; Stensola et al., 2012, 2015; Krupic et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an observation about the persistence of grid responses with citations to similar findings.

claim: Hypothesized functions of the grid system may be preserved even in the presence of grid distortions.
source: In fact, hypothesized functions of the grid system may be preserved even in the presence of grid distortions (Stemmler et al., 2015; Carpenter and Barry, 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical work.

claim: If small geometric idiosyncrasies of the inputs disproportionately contribute to triggering place-cell global remapping, then their consolidation could prove necessary for consistently recalling the correct place-cell map.
source: and if small geometric idiosyncrasies of the inputs disproportionately contribute to triggering place-cell global remapping—as entailed by theoretical models relating grid cells to place cells (Savelli and Knierim, 2010; Monaco et al., 2011)—then their consolidation could well prove necessary for consistently recalling the correct place-cell map.
evidence: This is a speculative functional interpretation based on theoretical models.

claim: In one rat, different grid maps were produced in identical cue configurations at the beginning and the end of the experimental day (STD vs. STD2).
source: A seeming counter-example to the involvement of grid framing in proper context recall was instead noticed in one rat in which different grid maps were produced in identical cue configurations at the beginning and the end of the experimental day (STD vs. STD2, Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This describes a specific observation that appears to contradict the general pattern.

claim: Even in the STD vs. STD2 case, a short-term memory process appeared at play, since the later grid map reflected the recent history of experimental interventions.
source: But even in this case a short-term memory process appeared at play, since we anecdotally found the later grid map to reflect the recent history of experimental interventions (Gupta et al., 2014), which could be regarded as a form of contextual discrimination.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the STD2 phenomenon with a citation to related work.

claim: The correction of path-integration errors required for stabilizing the grid could rely primarily on local boundaries even when room influence alters the geometric relationship between these boundaries and the grid.
source: In principle, the correction of path-integration errors required for stabilizing the grid could rely primarily on local boundaries (Giocomo, 2015; Hardcastle et al., 2015) even when room influence alters the geometric relationship between these boundaries and the grid, if the system has already learned the resulting grid-platform alignment for each manipulation.
evidence: This is a theoretical consideration about grid stabilization mechanisms.

claim: Stabilizing cues other than local boundaries seem necessary at least during the first experience of a manipulation before learning occurs.
source: However, because the manipulation-specific grid realignments observed in our experiments were not randomly generated, stabilizing cues other than local boundaries seem necessary at least during the first experience of a manipulation before this learning occurs.
evidence: This is an inference about the necessity of distal cues for initial grid stabilization.

claim: In the apparatus used, the distal visual landmarks on the room walls, or the room walls/boundaries themselves, were probably utilized to stabilize the grid in addition to local boundaries.
source: In our apparatus, the distal visual landmarks on the room walls, or the room walls/boundaries themselves, were probably utilized to stabilize the grid in addition to local boundaries.
evidence: This is an inference about which cues were used for grid stabilization in the experiments.

claim: Information about distal walls and landmarks may reach grid cells via boundary/landmark vector cells.
source: Information about distal walls and landmarks may reach grid cells via boundary/landmark vector cells (McNaughton et al., 1995; Hartley et al., 2000; Lever et al., 2009; Deshmukh and Knierim, 2013) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism for how distal cues influence grids, supported by citations.

claim: Alternatively, the grids might have relied on room cues to reset their orientation via the HD cell system, and on the geometric center of the platform to reset their phase.
source: Alternatively, the grids might have relied on room cues to reset their orientation via the HD cell system (Winter et al., 2015; Zugaro et al., 2001; Yoganarasimha et al., 2006; Knight et al., 2011; Clark et al., 2012), and on the geometric center of the platform to reset their phase.
evidence: This proposes an alternative mechanism for grid stabilization, supported by citations.

claim: Both alternatives for grid stabilization are consistent with the recent finding that grids in mice are destabilized in the dark, even when the HD signal is preserved.
source: Both alternatives are consistent with the recent finding that grids in mice are destabilized in the dark, even when the HD signal is preserved (Chen et al., 2016; see also Pérez-Escobar et al., 2016).
evidence: This connects the proposed mechanisms to recent experimental findings.

claim: Single-scale grid coupling is a built-in property of most attractor-network models of grid pattern generation.
source: Single-scale grid coupling is a built-in property of most attractor-network models of grid pattern generation (Fuhs and Touretzky, 2006; McNaughton et al., 2006; Bonnevie et al., 2013; Burak and Fiete, 2009).
evidence: This is a claim about theoretical models, supported by citations.

claim: By construction, all grid cells within the same attractor network have identical scale and orientation while their phase differences are determined by the fixed network connectivity.
source: By construction, all grid cells within the same attractor network have identical scale and orientation while their phase differences are determined by the (fixed) network connectivity; thus, the grids remain geometrically coupled no matter their collective response to environmental modifications.
evidence: This describes a property of attractor network models.

claim: Coordination of grids of different spacing seems to require extending attractor models with an explicit mechanism for interlocking multiple networks operating at different spatial scales.
source: However, coordination of grids of different spacing seems to require extending this model with an explicit mechanism for interlocking multiple networks operating at different spatial scales (Knierim and Zhang, 2012).
evidence: This is a theoretical inference about model requirements, supported by citation.

claim: Oscillatory models do not rely on an extensive network in their basic form and work by turning velocity-modulated temporal oscillations into grid-like spatial oscillations.
source: Oscillatory models (Burgess et al., 2007; Hasselmo et al., 2007; Blair et al., 2007), on the other hand, do not rely on an extensive network in their basic form. Because they essentially work by turning velocity-modulated temporal oscillations into grid-like spatial oscillations, synchronizing the former might in principle 'synchronize' the latter, thus spatially interlocking the grids.
evidence: This describes properties of oscillatory models with citations.

claim: Interlocked grids at different scales would require 'n:m' reciprocal entrainment in oscillatory models.
source: Interlocked grids at different scales would require 'n:m' reciprocal entrainment, by which n cycles of one rhythm correspond to m cycles of the other, possibly at different phase-lags (Zhang et al., 2009; Deshmukh et al., 2010; Belluscio et al., 2012; Brandon et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a theoretical requirement for oscillatory models, with citations to relevant work.

claim: Such a framework for multi-scale grid coordination in oscillatory models has not been explored.
source: Such a framework, to our knowledge, has not been explored (but Zilli and Hasselmo, 2010; Blair et al., 2014 investigated the synchronization of velocity-modulated oscillators for path-integration error-correction).
evidence: This identifies a gap in theoretical work with citations to related studies.

claim: In Hebbian learning models, the spacing of the grid depends on the time constant of the intrinsic adaptive dynamics.
source: In a third type of model, Hebbian learning of a grid-forming synaptic pattern is enabled by the spatiotemporal interaction of fast adaptive neural dynamics and spatial inputs that vary on a much slower behavioral timescale (Kropff and Treves, 2008; see also Franzius et al., 2007). The spacing of the grid depends on the time constant of the intrinsic adaptive dynamics.
evidence: This describes properties of Hebbian learning models with citations.

claim: Common orientation in a population of grid cells and invariance of reciprocal phase relationships in multiple environments can be achieved in Hebbian models by plastic collateral connections at the time of learning.
source: Common orientation in a population of grid cells and invariance of reciprocal phase relationships in multiple environments can be achieved in this model by plastic collateral connections at the time of learning (Si et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes a mechanism in Hebbian models, supported by citation.

claim: The extensions required of existing models to enable multi-scale interlocking could produce theoretical insights into the functional reasons for the quantal organization of the grid spacing.
source: Regardless of the class of models under consideration, the extensions required of existing models to enable multi-scale interlocking could produce theoretical insights into the functional reasons for the quantal organization of the grid spacing (Barry et al., 2007; Stensola et al., 2012; Knierim and Zhang, 2012; Stensola and Moser, 2016).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential theoretical insights, with citations.

claim: Stensola et al. (2012) observed a scale-dependent response of grid cells by compressing one axis of the enclosure: smaller-scale grids were 'chopped off' by the compressed apparatus, whereas larger-scale grids compressed along with it.
source: Further experimental and theoretical work is also needed to clarify the relationship between our observations and those by Stensola et al. (2012). Those investigators observed a scale-dependent response of grid cells by compressing one axis of the enclosure: smaller-scale grids were 'chopped off' by the compressed apparatus, whereas larger-scale grids compressed along with it.
evidence: This summarizes findings from a previous study.

claim: The mechanism responsible for the cross-scale grid coupling observed in the current data may not always be active.
source: Thus the mechanism responsible for the cross-scale grid coupling observed in our data may not always be active, and it is therefore unlikely to rely solely on genetically or developmentally hardwired networks.
evidence: This is an inference about the nature of the coupling mechanism based on comparison with previous findings.

claim: The cross-scale coupling mechanism may not apply to grid rescaling as it does to grid realignments.
source: Alternatively, this mechanism may not apply to grid rescaling as it does to grid realignments, as anecdotally suggested by a mildly divergent rescaling followed by tight geometric coupling in a pilot protocol we described (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on pilot data shown in a figure supplement.

claim: Eight male Long-Evans rats were used in the study.
source: Eight male Long-Evans rats (Harlan Sprague Dawley Inc., Indianapolis, IN) were housed individually on a 12:12 hr light-dark cycle
evidence: This describes the subjects used in the experiments.

claim: One rat was excluded from the analyses because its recordings did not yield any grid cells.
source: One rat was excluded from the analyses because its recordings did not yield any grid cells.
evidence: This explains why only seven rats are included in the results despite eight being used initially.

claim: The rats were 5 ½ –6 ½ months old and 470–590 g at the time of surgery.
source: The rats were 5 ½ –6 ½ months old and 470–590 g at the time of surgery.
evidence: This provides demographic information about the experimental subjects.

claim: Tetrodes were made by twisting 12.5 or 17 µm nichrome wire and electroplated with gold until the wire impedance was lowered to ~200 kOhms.
source: Tetrodes were made by twisting 12.5 or 17 µm nichrome wire (California Fine Wire Co., Grover Beach, CA). The tips were electroplated with gold, until the wire impedance was lowered to ~200 kOhms.
evidence: This describes the technical specifications of the recording electrodes.

claim: Rate maps were calculated in 3 × 3 cm bins.
source: The rat positions left in the unsmoothed trajectory were then binned in 3 × 3 cm bins to produce an occupancy map of the rat's dwell time in each bin.
evidence: This describes a methodological parameter for data analysis.

claim: Epochs of immobility or very slow locomotion (speed below 3 cm/s for longer than 500 ms) were excluded from rate map calculations.
source: Epochs of immobility or very slow locomotion were excluded from these calculations. To estimate the rat's speed, its trajectory was first smoothed by convolving both raw x,y position time series with a clipped Gaussian mask with variance = 300 ms. The mask values were renormalized at each step. Rat's speed in cm/s was calculated for each of the 30 Hz frame intervals based on the rat displacement between the two consecutive frames. Epochs longer than 500 ms, in which the speed remained below 3 cm/s, were expunged from the original, unsmoothed trajectory and from the spike train.
evidence: This describes a methodological criterion for data inclusion.

claim: Gridness scores for the rate maps eventually accepted by the selection procedure were generally far greater than 0.1 (mean 1.26 ± 0.28 S.D., 5%ile = 0.68, 95%ile = 1.58).
source: The gridness scores for the rate maps eventually accepted by this selection procedure were generally far greater than the 0.1 threshold used in steps 1 and 7 of the procedure (mean 1.26 ± 0.28 S.D., 5%ile = 0.68, 95%ile = 1.58).
evidence: This provides quantitative information about the quality of grid cells included in the analysis.

claim: 3780 rate maps from 1332 units recorded from seven rats in distinct sessions were subjected to the grid cell selection procedure.
source: 3780 rate maps from 1332 units recorded from seven rats in distinct sessions of the same day were subjected to the selection procedure.
evidence: This provides information about the total dataset size before selection.

claim: 758 rate maps from 308 units passed the grid cell selection procedure.
source: 758 rate maps from 308 units passed the selection: seven units in rat 262, 46 units in rat 263, 14 units in rat 292, 39 units in rat 332, 52 units in rat 334, 99 units in rat 377, 51 units in rat 387.
evidence: This provides information about the final dataset size after selection, broken down by rat.
